title_original: Lotus L. Kang Wins Canada’s Sobey Art Award
excerpt_original: The multidisciplinary artist, known for her evocative installations, clinched the CAD 100,000 (USD 70,000) top prize. Harison Butler

blocks.text: Lotus L. Kang Wins Canada’s Sobey Art Award

blocks.alt: Lotus L. Kang Wins Canada’s Sobey Art Award

blocks.text: LOTUS L. KANG . Photo by and copyright Carolyne Loreé Teston.

On November 14, Korean Canadian multidisciplinary artist Lotus L. Kang won the 2026 Sobey Art Award (SAA), Canada’s most prestigious contemporary art prize. Jointly presented by the National Gallery of Canada (NCC) and the Sobey Art Foundation, the accolade is endowed with CAD 100,000 (USD 70,000).

Born in 1985 in Toronto to Korean immigrants, Kang earned a BFA from Montreal’s Concordia University in 2008, followed by an MFA at the Milton Avery School of the Arts at Bard College, New York, in 2015. Her practice, spanning photography, installation, and sculpture, navigates themes of memory, inheritance, and impermanence. She is known for her installations comprising large, cascading sheets of unfixed industrial film, whose surfaces have “tanned” through overexposure, exploring concepts of decay and transformation. Kang’s work has been exhibited at various institutions across Canada and beyond—from London’s Chisenhale Gallery (2023) and Singapore’s Tanoto Art Foundation to the Frye Art Museum in Seattle (both 2026). A 2024 Guggenheim fellow, she also participated in the 15th Shanghai Biennale last year, and was chosen for the inaugural Bvlgari Pavilion at the 61st Venice Biennale with a site-specific commission. The latter installation, titled The face of desire is loss (2026), features her signature film “skins” alongside tatami mats, glass bottles, and bronze and fiberglass sculptures of kelp knots and birds within a glass chamber in the Giardini della Biennale, reflecting on Buddhist notions of death and rebirth.

Kang expressed her gratitude in a statement: “The recognition of this prize means that askew ideas are worth pursuing. Art is essential to life, progress, and love.” Jonathan Shaughnessy, director of NGC’s cultural initiatives and chair of the 2026 SAA jury, said the artist was selected for “the commitment and rigor demonstrated in her practice for well over a decade,” adding: “We celebrate the increasingly global reach of Kang’s poetic and beautiful work, which presents an active reflection on our contemporary moment.”

Established in 1981 by Canadian art collector Frank H. Sobey, the Sobey Art Award is dedicated to supporting emerging and midcareer contemporary artists from Canada and beyond. The five other artists shortlisted for this year’s edition—Melaw Nakehk’o, Samuel Roy-Bois, Audie Murray, Caroline Monnet, and Shane Perley-Dutcher—each took home a CAD 25,000 (USD 17,500) prize.
Harison Butler is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
